# Limits of Functions

::: {.callout-note}
## Companion reading
This lecture corresponds to C&J §1.8 (the concept of limit for a function of a continuous
variable), tying together §1.2.d (continuity) with the Intermediate Value Theorem of §1.2.e.
:::

## From Sequences to Functions

We already know what it means for a *sequence* to converge (@def-limit). We now transfer this idea
to functions: instead of asking what happens to $a_n$ as $n\to\infty$, we ask what happens to
$f(x)$ as $x$ approaches some fixed point $a$. The cheapest way to make this precise is to reduce it
to something we already understand — sequences — by feeding *every* sequence approaching $a$ into
$f$ and demanding that the outputs all converge to the same value.

::: {#def-function-limit}
\
Let $f\colon D\to\R$ with $D\subseteq\R$, and let $a\in\R$. We say
$$
\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L
$$
if for **every** sequence $(x_n)$ with $x_n\in D$, $x_n\neq a$, and $x_n\to a$, we have
$f(x_n)\to L$.
:::

::: {#rem-function-limit-every-sequence}
The word "every" is doing all the work: it is not enough to find *some* sequence $x_n\to a$ with
$f(x_n)\to L$ — the same $L$ must come out no matter which approaching sequence we feed in. This
mirrors uniqueness of sequential limits (@rem-limit-unique): if two different sequences $x_n\to a$
and $x_n'\to a$ produced different outputs $f(x_n)\to L$ and $f(x_n')\to L'\neq L$, the limit
$\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ would simply not exist.
:::

::: {#exm-x-squared-function-limit}
\
Let $f(x) = x^2$. Then $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0} f(x) = 0$.

::: {.proof}
Let $(x_n)$ be an arbitrary sequence with $x_n\to 0$. We may assume $\abs{x_n}\le 1$ for all $n$
(true eventually, since $x_n\to0$). Then
$$
0 \le f(x_n) = x_n^2 \le \abs{x_n},
$$
and $\abs{x_n}\to 0$, so by the comparison test (@prp-comparison), $x_n^2 \to 0$. Since $(x_n)$ was
an arbitrary sequence converging to $0$, @def-function-limit gives $\lim_{x\to0} f(x) = 0$.
:::
:::

## The $\eps$–$\delta$ Version

Just as with continuity (@def-continuity), the sequential definition of a function limit has an
equivalent $\eps$–$\delta$ formulation.

::: {#prp-function-limit-eps-delta}
## $\eps$–$\delta$ characterization of a limit
Let $f\colon D\to\R$, $a\in\R$, $L\in\R$. Then
$$
\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L
\Iff
\text{for every } \eps>0 \text{ there exists } \delta>0 \text{ s.t. }
x\in D,\ 0<\abs{x-a}<\delta \Imp \abs{f(x)-L}<\eps.
$$
:::

The proof is the same idea as the equivalence used implicitly for continuity: if the $\eps$–$\delta$
condition holds and $x_n\to a$, choosing $N$ so that $\abs{x_n-a}<\delta$ for $n\ge N$ forces
$\abs{f(x_n)-L}<\eps$ for $n\ge N$, i.e. $f(x_n)\to L$. Conversely, if the $\eps$–$\delta$ condition
*fails* for some $\eps>0$, then for every $\delta = \tfrac1n$ we can pick a point $x_n$ with
$0<\abs{x_n-a}<\tfrac1n$ but $\abs{f(x_n)-L}\ge\eps$ — producing a sequence $x_n\to a$ with
$f(x_n)\not\to L$, so the sequential definition fails too.

The only difference from @def-continuity is the punctured condition $0<\abs{x-a}$: a limit does not
care what happens (or fails to happen) *at* $a$ itself, only nearby. This is what lets us connect
the two notions.

::: {#prp-continuity-via-limit}
## Continuity, restated
Let $f\colon D\to\R$ and $a\in D$. Then $f$ is continuous at $a$ (@def-continuity) if and only if
$$
\lim_{x\to a} f(x) \text{ exists and equals } f(a).
$$
:::

This is exactly @def-continuity with the roles of $x$ and $a$ relabeled: continuity says
$\abs{x-a}<\delta \Imp \abs{f(x)-f(a)}<\eps$, which is the $\eps$–$\delta$ condition of
@prp-function-limit-eps-delta with $L=f(a)$ (the point $x=a$ itself trivially satisfies
$\abs{f(x)-f(a)}=0<\eps$, so punctured and unpunctured versions agree once $L=f(a)$).

## Examples

::: {#exm-cube-continuous}
\
$f(x) = x^3$ is continuous at every $a\in\R$.

::: {.proof}
Let $x_n\to a$. By the limit laws for sequences (@prp-limit-laws),
$$
x_n^3 = x_n\cdot x_n\cdot x_n \longrightarrow a\cdot a\cdot a = a^3.
$$
Hence $f(x_n)\to f(a)$ for every sequence $x_n\to a$, so $\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = f(a)$, and
@prp-continuity-via-limit gives continuity at $a$.
:::
:::

::: {#exm-dirichlet-discontinuous}
\
The **Dirichlet function**
$$
f(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & x\in\Q \\ 0 & x\notin\Q \end{cases}
$$
is discontinuous at every $a\in\R$.

Take $a=1$. Consider the two sequences
$$
x_n = 1+\frac1n \quad(\text{rational}), \qquad\qquad y_n = 1+\frac{\sqrt2}{n} \quad(\text{irrational}).
$$
Both converge to $1$, but
$$
f(x_n) \equiv 1 \to 1, \qquad\qquad f(y_n) \equiv 0 \to 0 \neq f(1) = 1.
$$
Since two sequences converging to $a=1$ produce different limits for $f$, $\lim_{x\to1}f(x)$ does not
exist (@rem-function-limit-every-sequence), so $f$ is not continuous at $1$.
:::

::: {#exr-dirichlet-general-a}
Adapt the argument of @exm-dirichlet-discontinuous to an arbitrary $a\in\R$: exhibit a rational
sequence and an irrational sequence, both converging to $a$, on which the Dirichlet function takes
different limiting values. Conclude that $f$ is discontinuous at *every* $a\in\R$.
:::

::: {#exm-piecewise-jump}
\
Let
$$
f(x) = \begin{cases} x^3+16 & x<0 \\ -2x+3 & x\ge 0. \end{cases}
$$
Take $x_n = -\tfrac1n \to 0$. Then
$$
f(x_n) = \left(-\frac1n\right)^{\!3} + 16 \longrightarrow 16 \neq f(0) = 3,
$$
so $f$ is discontinuous at $0$. We will see below exactly what kind of discontinuity this is.
:::

## One-Sided Limits

For @exm-piecewise-jump, the failure of continuity comes from the two "branches" of $f$ disagreeing
at $0$ — approaching from the left gives a different answer than approaching from the right. To
capture this we restrict which sequences $x_n\to a$ we are allowed to test with.

::: {#def-one-sided-limits}
\
Let $f\colon D\to\R$ and $a\in\R$.

- $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a^-} f(x) = L$ (the **left-sided limit**) if $f(x_n)\to L$ for every
  *increasing* sequence $x_n \nearrow a$ with $x_n\in D$.
- $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a^+} f(x) = L$ (the **right-sided limit**) if $f(x_n)\to L$ for every
  *decreasing* sequence $x_n \searrow a$ with $x_n\in D$.
:::

::: {#rem-one-sided-disagree}
The left- and right-sided limits may disagree. For $f$ as in @exm-piecewise-jump,
$$
\lim_{x\to0^-} f(x) = 16, \qquad\qquad \lim_{x\to0^+} f(x) = 3,
$$
since $x^3+16\to16$ along any $x_n\nearrow0$, while $-2x+3\to3$ along any $x_n\searrow0$.
:::

::: {#def-jump-discontinuity}
\
$f$ has a **jump discontinuity** at $a$ if both one-sided limits exist and are finite, but
$$
\lim_{x\to a^-} f(x) \neq \lim_{x\to a^+} f(x).
$$
This makes precise the informal description from @rem-jump-discontinuity, and excludes the
unbounded case of @rem-infinite-discontinuity, where no finite one-sided limit exists at all. The
function of @exm-piecewise-jump has a jump discontinuity at $0$.
:::

::: {#thm-continuity-one-sided}
\
Let $f\colon D\to\R$ and $a\in D$. Then $f$ is continuous at $a$ if and only if
$$
\lim_{x\to a^-} f(x) = f(a) = \lim_{x\to a^+} f(x).
$$
:::

Like the two-sided limit (@prp-function-limit-eps-delta), each one-sided limit has an equivalent
$\eps$–$\delta$ form obtained by restricting to one side:
$$
\lim_{x\to a^-} f(x) = L \Iff \forall\eps>0\ \exists\delta>0:\ a-\delta<x<a \Imp \abs{f(x)-L}<\eps,
$$
and symmetrically for $\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=L$ with $a<x<a+\delta$.

::: {.proof}
If $f$ is continuous at $a$, then $f(x_n)\to f(a)$ for *every* sequence $x_n\to a$
(@prp-continuity-via-limit) — in particular for every increasing sequence $x_n\nearrow a$ and every
decreasing sequence $x_n\searrow a$, giving both one-sided limits equal to $f(a)$.

Conversely, suppose both one-sided limits equal $f(a)$, and let $\eps>0$. By the $\eps$–$\delta$
forms above there exist $\delta_1,\delta_2>0$ with
$$
a-\delta_1<x<a \Imp \abs{f(x)-f(a)}<\eps, \qquad\qquad a<x<a+\delta_2 \Imp \abs{f(x)-f(a)}<\eps.
$$
Let $\delta=\min(\delta_1,\delta_2)$. If $0<\abs{x-a}<\delta$, then either $a-\delta<x<a$ or
$a<x<a+\delta$, so in both cases $\abs{f(x)-f(a)}<\eps$; and $x=a$ trivially gives
$\abs{f(x)-f(a)}=0<\eps$. So $\abs{x-a}<\delta \Imp \abs{f(x)-f(a)}<\eps$, which is exactly
@def-continuity.
:::

## Limit Laws for Functions

Because @def-function-limit reduces everything to sequences, the arithmetic of function limits
carries over directly from the arithmetic of sequence limits (@prp-limit-laws).

::: {#prp-function-limit-laws}
## Arithmetic of function limits
Suppose $\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L$ and $\lim_{x\to a} g(x) = M$. Then
$$
\lim_{x\to a} \big(f(x)+g(x)\big) = L+M, \qquad\qquad \lim_{x\to a} f(x)g(x) = LM,
$$
and, if $M\neq0$,
$$
\lim_{x\to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{L}{M}.
$$
:::

::: {#cor-continuity-algebra}
If $a\in\dom(f)\cap\dom(g)$ and $f,g$ are continuous at $a$, then $f+g$, $f\cdot g$, and (provided
$g(a)\neq0$) $f/g$ are continuous at $a$.
:::

::: {#exm-rational-function-limit}
\
$$
\lim_{x\to 0} \frac{x^3-3x+4}{x^2+\cos(x)}
= \frac{\lim_{x\to0}x^3 - \lim_{x\to0}3x + \lim_{x\to0}4}{\lim_{x\to0}x^2 + \lim_{x\to0}\cos(x)}
= \frac{0-0+4}{0+1} = 4.
$$
:::

::: {#exm-quotient-careful}
\
**Careful:** the quotient rule requires the *denominator's* limit to be nonzero — it says nothing
when both numerator and denominator vanish. For
$$
\lim_{x\to a} \frac{x^2-a^2}{x-a},
$$
we have $\lim_{x\to a}(x-a) = 0$, so @prp-function-limit-laws simply does not apply. Instead,
factor first:
$$
\frac{x^2-a^2}{x-a} = \frac{(x-a)(x+a)}{x-a} = x+a \qquad (x\neq a),
$$
and only *then* take the limit: $\lim_{x\to a}(x+a) = 2a$.
:::

## The Intermediate Value Theorem

::: {#thm-ivt}
## Intermediate Value Theorem
Let $f\colon\R\to\R$ be continuous, and suppose $a<b$ with $f(a)<0$ and $f(b)>0$. Then there exists
$c\in(a,b)$ with $f(c)=0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
We construct $c$ by **bisection**. Set $a_1=a$, $b_1=b$, so $f(a_1)\le0\le f(b_1)$. Given $a_n,b_n$
with $f(a_n)\le0$ and $f(b_n)\ge0$, let $m_n = \tfrac{a_n+b_n}{2}$.

- If $f(m_n)=0$, we are done — take $c=m_n$.
- If $f(m_n)<0$, set $a_{n+1}=m_n$, $b_{n+1}=b_n$.
- If $f(m_n)>0$, set $a_{n+1}=a_n$, $b_{n+1}=m_n$.

In either of the last two cases $f(a_{n+1})\le0\le f(b_{n+1})$, so the invariant is preserved, and we
continue. If the process never terminates, this produces sequences with $(a_n)$ increasing,
$(b_n)$ decreasing, $a_n\le b_n$ for all $n$, and
$$
b_n - a_n = \frac{b-a}{2^{n-1}} \longrightarrow 0
$$
(the interval length halves at each step; compare @exr-warmup-half-n). By @cor-monotone-squeeze,
$(a_n)$ and $(b_n)$ converge to a common limit $c\in[a,b]$.

Since $f$ is continuous, @prp-continuity-via-limit gives $f(a_n)\to f(c)$ and $f(b_n)\to f(c)$. Now
$f(a_n)\le0$ for every $n$; if we had $f(c)>0$, taking $\eps=f(c)/2$ in the definition of
convergence would force $f(a_n)>f(c)/2>0$ for large $n$, a contradiction. So $f(c)\le0$. The same
argument with $f(b_n)\ge0$ gives $f(c)\ge0$. Hence $f(c)=0$, and $a<c<b$ since $f(a)<0$ and
$f(b)>0$ rule out $c=a$ or $c=b$.
:::

::: {#rem-ivt-general}
The same bisection idea proves the more general statement: if $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $y$
lies between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, then $f(c)=y$ for some $c\in[a,b]$ — apply @thm-ivt to $f(x)-y$.
:::

## Summary

- $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L$ (@def-function-limit) means $f(x_n)\to L$ for **every**
  sequence $x_n\to a$ in $\dom(f)$ — this reduces function limits to sequence limits, and is
  equivalent to the $\eps$–$\delta$ condition of @prp-function-limit-eps-delta.
- **Continuity restated:** $f$ is continuous at $a$ exactly when $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ exists and
  equals $f(a)$ (@prp-continuity-via-limit).
- **One-sided limits** (@def-one-sided-limits) test only monotone sequences approaching from one
  side. A **jump discontinuity** (@def-jump-discontinuity) is exactly a point where both one-sided
  limits exist (finitely) but disagree; $f$ is continuous at $a$ iff both one-sided limits equal
  $f(a)$ (@thm-continuity-one-sided).
- The **limit laws** (@prp-function-limit-laws) compute limits of sums, products, and quotients
  termwise, and give continuity of $f+g$, $f\cdot g$, $f/g$ from continuity of $f$ and $g$
  (@cor-continuity-algebra) — but a $\tfrac00$ form must be simplified *before* the quotient rule
  applies (@exm-quotient-careful).
- The **Intermediate Value Theorem** (@thm-ivt): a continuous function that is negative at $a$ and
  positive at $b$ must vanish somewhere in between. The proof bisects $[a,b]$ into nested intervals
  shrinking to a point $c$, then uses continuity to pass $f(a_n)\le0\le f(b_n)$ to the limit.
